subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A healthy 20-year-old college student has a routine physical examination. The first heart sound is single, but the second heart sound is heard as two distinct components when she inhales deeply and as a single sound when she exhales.
question: Which of the following best explains the inspiratory separation of the second heart sound in this patient?

options.text: Inspiration raises intrathoracic pressure, which decreases venous return and shortens right ventricular ejection
Inspiration drops intrathoracic pressure, which increases venous return, right ventricular filling and ejection time, delaying pulmonic valve closure
Inspiration increases left-sided filling, which lengthens left ventricular ejection and delays aortic valve closure
Inspiration decreases pulmonary vascular impedance and left atrial volume, delaying closure of the mitral valve
Inspiration increases flow across an atrial septal defect, delaying pulmonic closure independently of respiration

explanation_correct: Physiologic splitting of S2 occurs because inspiration lowers intrathoracic pressure, which increases venous return to the right heart. Greater right ventricular filling increases right ventricular stroke volume and ejection time, delaying closure of the pulmonic valve (P2). In addition, inspiration decreases pulmonary impedance (increases the capacity of the pulmonary circulation), which further contributes to delayed pulmonic closure. The split disappears on expiration, exactly as described in this healthy student.

explanation_incorrect.A: Inspiration lowers, not raises, intrathoracic pressure and increases, rather than decreases, venous return; the resulting longer right ventricular ejection delays, not shortens, P2.
explanation_incorrect.C: Inspiration decreases venous return to the left heart, so left ventricular ejection is not prolonged; aortic closure (A2) is the earlier sound in physiologic splitting.
explanation_incorrect.D: Decreased pulmonary impedance does contribute to delayed pulmonic closure, but this option wrongly ties it to delayed mitral closure; the mitral valve is not involved in S2 splitting.
explanation_incorrect.E: Flow through an atrial septal defect producing respiration-independent (fixed) splitting describes ASD, not the normal respiration-dependent split heard in this healthy patient.

educationalObjective: Physiologic splitting of S2 is due to inspiration increasing RV filling and ejection time (plus decreased pulmonary impedance), delaying pulmonic valve closure.

subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A 30-year-old woman is found to have a persistently split second heart sound that does not change with respiration. She reports palpitations, and an echocardiogram is obtained. The examiner notes that the separation between the aortic and pulmonic components is identical during inspiration and expiration.
question: Which of the following mechanisms most likely explains this patient's fixed splitting of S2?

options.text: Delayed left ventricular depolarization prolongs left ventricular ejection, postponing aortic valve closure
Obstruction at the aortic valve prolongs left ventricular ejection time, reversing the order of semilunar closure
Delayed right ventricular depolarization prolongs right ventricular ejection, exaggerating the normal inspiratory widening
Elevated pericardial pressure prevents early diastolic filling, holding both semilunar closure times constant
A left-to-right shunt increases right atrial and right ventricular volumes, raising flow through the pulmonic valve and delaying its closure regardless of respiration

explanation_correct: Fixed splitting of S2 is heard in atrial septal defect. The ASD creates a left-to-right shunt that increases right atrial and right ventricular volumes, which increases flow through the pulmonic valve and delays pulmonic valve closure. Because this extra volume is present continuously, the delay is independent of respiration, producing a split that is unchanged between inspiration and expiration.

explanation_incorrect.A: Delayed left ventricular depolarization (left bundle branch block) delays aortic closure and produces paradoxical splitting, in which P2 precedes A2, not fixed splitting.
explanation_incorrect.B: Aortic valve obstruction (aortic stenosis) delays aortic closure and also produces paradoxical splitting; it does not create a respiration-independent wide split with normal valve order.
explanation_incorrect.C: Delayed right ventricular depolarization (right bundle branch block) causes wide splitting that still varies with respiration—an exaggeration of normal—rather than a fixed split.
explanation_incorrect.D: Elevated pericardial pressure describes cardiac tamponade, which affects the y descent of the JVP and does not hold semilunar valve closure times constant.

educationalObjective: Fixed splitting of S2 is characteristic of ASD: a left-to-right shunt increases flow through the pulmonic valve, delaying P2 independent of respiration.

subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A 70-year-old man presents 4 days after a myocardial infarction. The second heart sound is split at rest and the split becomes even wider when he inhales. The QRS duration on his ECG is prolonged, with a broad S wave in lead I and a broad R wave in lead V1.
question: Which of the following best explains the wide splitting of S2 in this patient?

options.text: Delayed activation of the right ventricle prolongs right ventricular emptying, delaying pulmonic valve closure beyond the normal inspiratory delay
Delayed activation of the left ventricle prolongs left ventricular emptying, delaying aortic valve closure until after the pulmonic component
Increased flow through the pulmonic valve from a left-to-right shunt delays pulmonic closure independently of respiration
Obstruction of the left ventricular outflow tract prolongs left ventricular ejection, postponing aortic closure
Inspiration-induced decrease in pulmonary impedance keeps the pulmonic valve open longer during both inspiration and expiration

explanation_correct: The ECG findings describe a right bundle branch block, which delays right ventricular depolarization and therefore right ventricular emptying, delaying pulmonic valve closure. This produces wide splitting—especially pronounced on inspiration—and is an exaggeration of normal splitting. Right bundle branch block is one of the classic causes of wide splitting, along with pulmonic stenosis.

explanation_incorrect.B: Delayed left ventricular activation describes left bundle branch block, which delays aortic closure and produces paradoxical splitting with P2 before A2, not wide splitting.
explanation_incorrect.C: A left-to-right shunt increasing pulmonic flow describes atrial septal defect, which produces fixed splitting that does not widen further with inspiration.
explanation_incorrect.D: Left ventricular outflow obstruction (aortic stenosis) delays aortic valve closure and causes paradoxical, not wide, splitting.
explanation_incorrect.E: Decreased pulmonary impedance on inspiration contributes to normal physiologic splitting, but it does not keep the pulmonic valve open during expiration; the ECG conduction abnormality explains this patient's persistent widening.

educationalObjective: Wide splitting of S2 occurs with delayed RV emptying, classically right bundle branch block or pulmonic stenosis, and widens further on inspiration.

subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A 75-year-old man with a harsh crescendo-decrescendo murmur radiating to the carotids has an abnormal second heart sound: the sound is split while he exhales, and the split disappears while he inhales. Careful auscultation shows that the component that closes later is the one that becomes single during inspiration.
question: Which of the following best describes the mechanism of this patient's abnormal S2 splitting?

options.text: Increased right-sided flow from a left-to-right shunt delays pulmonic closure so much that the split no longer varies with respiration
Delayed right ventricular depolarization prolongs right ventricular ejection, widening the normal inspiratory separation further
Inspiration increases right ventricular filling so pulmonic closure is further delayed, splitting the sound on inspiration and merging it on expiration
Delayed aortic valve closure reverses the normal order of semilunar closure so that P2 precedes A2; on inspiration P2 moves closer to A2, eliminating the split heard on expiration
Decreased pulmonary impedance on expiration delays pulmonic closure, producing a split that is present only during expiration

explanation_correct: This patient has paradoxical splitting, heard in conditions that delay aortic valve closure, such as aortic stenosis (his murmur) and left bundle branch block. The normal order of semilunar valve closure is reversed, so P2 occurs before A2. During inspiration, pulmonic closure is normally delayed and P2 moves closer to the already-delayed A2, 'paradoxically' eliminating the split; the split is therefore audible on expiration—opposite to physiologic splitting.

explanation_incorrect.A: A respiration-independent split describes fixed splitting from ASD, in which pulmonic closure is delayed by increased transvalvular flow, not by delayed aortic closure.
explanation_incorrect.B: Delayed right ventricular depolarization (right bundle branch block) produces wide splitting that widens further with inspiration—the opposite pattern of this patient.
explanation_incorrect.C: This describes physiologic splitting, in which the split is heard on inspiration and disappears on expiration; this patient's split is heard on expiration and disappears on inspiration.
explanation_incorrect.E: Decreased pulmonary impedance occurs during inspiration, not expiration, and its effect is incorporated into the physiologic-splitting mechanism, not the reversed-valve-order pattern seen here.

educationalObjective: Paradoxical splitting (aortic stenosis, LBBB) reverses semilunar closure order so P2 precedes A2; inspiration moves P2 closer to A2 and eliminates the split heard on expiration.
